speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I was young, I was a regular visitor to the National Library at Stamford Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The National Library allowed me to read books and to find out more about the world without having to take a single step out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recall spending hours at the old National Library reading fictional books, books about playing chess, stories about Greek mythology and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the National Library at Stamford Road was torn down in 2005 to make way for Fort Canning Tunnel, I was very disappointed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The National Library was a building which carries many fond memories not just for myself but for many other Singaporeans around my age group.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I can still recall eating ice kacang from the stall full of bees flying around at the coffeeshop.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sadly, those memories of my time as a young boy at the Stamford Road National Library would now only remain as memories.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I had lived at Rochor Centre from 1977 to 1990.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I shifted there when I was in Secondary 2 when it was a new block of flats and lived there until I married and moved out.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I spent the better part of my growing up years in that estate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the years, we have seen the demolition and loss of other prominent buildings like the National Theatre, the Van Kleef Aquarium and Queensway Cinema.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Prominent places like New World, Gay World, Great World – they are all gone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The old Bugis Street, Chinatown and Sungei Road are also all gone and, in their places, we have commercial buildings and shopping complexes, many of which lack the original identity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Critics say that they all look similar to other buildings and shopping complexes which can be found all over Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recognise that Singapore needs to progress and development has to take place.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, when Singaporeans experience loss of too many familiar buildings, familiar places of entertainment and environment, there will be this sense of loss of roots, a loss of emotional attachment to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Museums should not be the only repositories of a nation's memories and history.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our children and the future generation should not be left to read about Singapore's heritage, culture and history Page: 68 only through history textbooks, photographs or some heritage trails.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our future generation should have the opportunity to walk through and experience for themselves the same places which their parents had previously walked through, to allow them to experience and feel the presence of a particular environment of a local culture.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Just to cite an example, I can show a person a picture book of the Botanic Gardens, or even take him on an interactive journey on the computer to explore the Botanic Gardens, but it is never the same as taking him to the Botanic Gardens for a walk in the park to admire the rainforest, the Ginger Garden, the majestic Tembusu tree or to watch the swans at the lake.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One way to do so is to identify the collective memories of Singaporeans and to see how we can preserve the existing way of life and the local identity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Old buildings like the National Library, National Theatre, Van Kleef Aquarium; places like Sungei Road, Chinatown, Little India, Bugis Street; they all form part of the culture and heritage of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are the buildings and places which existed during the days of nation building.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They are all part of the Singapore history.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many other countries are also taking steps to preserve their heritage and culture.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Just look at the efforts by Japan, Hong Kong and the countries in Europe.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Try as we may, we may never be able to re-create the same culture, the same setting.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Just look at Chinatown and Bugis Street as examples of our attempts to re-create the environment and setting but which did not succeed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One of my concerns is that when a Singaporean leaves the country to work or study for a few years, when he returns, the place becomes unrecognisable because new buildings keep sprouting up and older buildings get demolished.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Prof Tommy Koh, in a recent speech at the World Cities Summit, said, "History and culture can play an important role in the rejuvenation of cities and in transforming ordinary cities into great cities." Prof Koh said that "the Singapore conservation movement came in time to realise the importance of conserving our built heritage and the anchors of our individual and collective memories".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This brings me to the question: how does the Government balance between developing our country for better progress as against preserving our heritage, culture and history?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Government help citizens to develop a greater sense of belonging to Singapore by preserving more of our history, more of our culture and more of our heritage buildings?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I raised this matter in 2015 in a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And plans for the redevelopment of Dakota Crescent were made known sometime in 2014.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After the announcement, HDB started to brief the residents about their relocation options and the plan to move the residents to a new block of rental flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During this period, many residents came to share with me that they will miss the place after staying in Dakota Crescent for more than 50 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have so many stories to tell and so many memories attached to the place.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Page: 69 Even people whom I have not met before came up to me to share that they had lived in the estate when they were young.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They can recall their days growing up in the Old Airport estate and Dakota area.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometime in 2015, several residents approached me to argue that there is sufficient merit for the Government to consider preserving Dakota Crescent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I met these residents and other interested parties to better understand their viewpoint.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After hearing them out, I agreed with them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a tranquil place located next to the river.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, I would invite Members of the House to drop by there one day just to walk in the evening, very tranquil.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To many Singaporeans who pass by Old Airport Road regularly, they call the flats the "seven-storey houses", or what they say in Hokkien, "qi lao chu".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Dakota Crescent is one of the first public housing projects built during the SIT era to provide mass housing just before the role of mass building for the public was passed on to HDB.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The fact that this estate is older than Singapore is a cause for celebration and should be an important consideration for conservation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The estate was named after a Dakota plane crashed at Kallang Airport.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I was also told that in 1959, the Constitution Exposition was held at Kallang Airport to commemorate internal self-government in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It was a spectacular exhibition and a huge celebration at that time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Dakota Crescent was witness to this exhibition as it was situated just next to Kallang Airport.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This report is a ground-up movement from interested residents who feel passionately that Dakota Crescent should be preserved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the Conservation Report, they shared more about the architectural, historical and social significance of Dakota Crescent and the rationale for wanting to preserve this unique piece of estate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is very interesting to learn more about the uniqueness of the design of the flats from an architectural point of view.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Conservation Report shared about how Dakota can be used to become a space for educating the future generation about Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are suggestions as to how the estate can be re-developed for use by arts groups, social enterprises, or as rental flats for couples waiting for their BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, this is not just a call by residents to conserve the place.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have even taken the effort to share more about how the Government can use the space even as we conserve it.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of these suggestions warrant serious consideration by the town planners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that by speaking on this Motion, I can persuade the Government to re-think its redevelopment plans for Dakota Crescent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe that this Government can do more to preserve our heritage, culture and history.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And by preserving key portions of a unique neighbourhood like Dakota Crescent, the Government would encourage cultural and social networks to be involved and to thrive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This, Mdm Speaker, I submit, would make Singapore a better place for all our future generations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In 1996, the Wychwood Barns, a complex of five tram sheds constructed in 1913 for the Toronto Civic Railway was slated for demolishment and the land where it sat on was to be sold.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While the Barns was an important transit facility from the 1920s to the 1940s, when trams were phased out, this unique red-brick complex was decommissioned, unattended to and soon degenerated into disrepair.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, fearful of what might be redeveloped on the site, local City Councillor Joe Mihevc and some of his residents around the area decided to act quickly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Barn was opened for residents to visit and acquaint themselves with the space.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many were awed by the structure, its high ceiling and its enchanting red bricks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The community rallied together, requesting that a Heritage and Environmental Impact assessment be conducted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: People gathered together over many sessions to discuss plans for the building and the land.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The residents also engaged Artscape, a non-profit organisation that engaged in real estate and programme development for the arts and creative sector, to help develop ideas.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The conversations and the consultations took many years and the final proposal was only ready in 2005.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I visited the Barn in 2014 and was awed by what it has become.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are many other such amazing creative place-making projects, like Project Row House in Houston, Pillsbury House in Minnesota.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I quoted these examples because they have so much resonance with what my fellow parliamentarian Mr Lim Biow Chuan has shared in his speech.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am supportive of his Motion and the effort to champion this important cause for two very important reasons.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One, redevelopment with cultural assets as a resource.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What the conservationists are arguing for is development that takes heritage as our cultural asset into consideration such that heritage becomes a resource for development.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As we strive to become a more liveable, sustainable city state, such cultural assets should be a key component for redevelopment because they can serve to enhance its overall value.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Conservation of precincts, such as Dakota Crescent, allows us to protect and promote our identity as a nation with rich and complex identities, histories and narratives – all of which are traits that not only make us interesting and exciting, but also show our resilience and the relevance of our historical development to our success today.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 71 While demolishment may be the cheapest solution or the easiest one, we lose not just tangible assets like buildings but also intangible cultural assets, historical narratives and memories.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some may say that history can be told through books and photographs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Joe Mihevc, the Toronto City Councillor who led the ground-up effort to transform the Wychwood Barn, reflected, "If there is one key lesson to be learnt it is that positive things happen when Torontonians step up and take charge.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The passion and dedication of hundreds of people created a critical web of support.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Together, with each holding a piece of the puzzle and needing the cooperation of the others to make it happen, the Barns project was an unstoppable force." Going back to the case of Dakota Crescent.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When news that the SIT flats of Dakota Crescent would make way for future development, Singaporeans and residents of Dakota very quickly responded.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: People visited Dakota Crescent to take pictures of the quaint little estate, artists came to create engagement projects to document what was valuable about Dakota.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some, like Dakota Adventures, helped people to understand more about the area.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Others, such as residents like Jonathan Poh, organised themselves and envisioned a different future for Dakota Crescent.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly, for many Singaporeans, city-building is not merely about the physical or architectural side of projects.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, they saw and valued intangible assets of the precinct, personal relationships and organisation within the community, meaning-making of the space they lived in and were proud of it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In short, what we witnessed was a case of citizens who want to take ownership of their community and history.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And their sense of ownership is what makes for successful development.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the proposal has the makings of a successful place-making project.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One, it has leadership and ownership from the community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The proposal is spearheaded by a community that has rallied together through a common recognition of a cultural asset of the precinct and a desire to enhance this value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Others may not quite be so historic, but they have become a part of many Singaporeans' lives and we have formed collective precious memories about such buildings and about such places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If we can keep and protect these buildings, they can help build a deeper sense of identity and rootedness for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In master-planning our land-scarce city-state, our planners have many considerations to address.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to provide for housing, medical facilities, schools, sports facilities, social amenities, religious and civic space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We need space for economic purposes to create jobs for Singaporeans, space for transport, land for nature reserves, parks, greenery and the list goes on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Given these tight constraints, the need to redevelop and rejuvenate our city will always be present.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But increasingly, the challenge we have to throw at ourselves is whether we can keep our city vibrant and dynamic and cater to the needs of Singaporeans while retaining that sense of time and space, that feeling of familiarity and nostalgia even amid change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In short, the question is, can we develop without sacrificing our identity and our heritage?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And can we conserve without stalling progress and change?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The answer, I think, must lie in striking the right balance, between preserving our past and catering to the needs of the present and the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Kok talked about cultural planning where both development and conservation can co-exist.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think these are solutions that increasingly we have to find.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When we do our work, our focus is not just to plan and build new infrastructure but to undertake development in a way that is sensitive to nature and to our past, and to build stronger emotional connections with our city.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is why, over the years, we have placed more emphasis on the conservation of buildings as an integral part of our urban master plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And for Kampong Glam, some of you may know, there is actually a community committee, both of people who live there, people who run businesses there, stakeholders who are interested in heritage, culture and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This process of identifying buildings and sites for conservation is an extensive and rigorous one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is not just based on nostalgic or sentimental value alone, but, importantly, we take into account the historical and heritage significance of the buildings, as well as their architectural merit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Page: 73 We also involve many stakeholders in the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: MND and URA take in feedback from our Conservation Advisory Panel (CAP), local community groups and also members of the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This survey includes research and documentation of buildings and sites of historic or cultural interest found in Singapore and completed in and before 1980.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will also allow us to be better informed when drawing up future land-use plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even after deciding to conserve a building, much research and documentation work still needs to be carried out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In particular, URA will study how the building can be adapted for re-use and contribute meaningfully to the plans for the larger area, while being sensitive to the history of the conserved building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As far as possible, we look for ways to enhance the overall heritage value of the place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One example is Balestier, which is a key identity node because of its strong heritage value and distinctive old world charm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The area is rich in history and home to an interesting mix of conserved pre- and post-war shophouses and the Sun Yat Sen Nanyang Memorial Hall, which is a National Monument.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The unique hotel-park development synergises with the Sun Yat Sen Nanyang Memorial Hall and the surrounding heritage shophouses, adding to the vibrancy of the larger Balestier area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, the area continues to be bustling with people visiting the heritage buildings, Zhongshan Park as the new park is called, and going to the area for lighting and hardware shops and, of course, not forgetting the famous "Tau Sar Piah" in the Balestier area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I highlight this example because heritage conservation work does not stop when buildings are gazetted and protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Otherwise, they risk collecting dust and melting into obscurity and people will forget about them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The intangible dimensions of our heritage are, in fact, also an important part of our shared identity and provide a link between the past and the present and, hopefully, with the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Intangible cultural heritage can refer to the festivals we celebrate and the diverse aspects of our traditions and our culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These cultural expressions of living heritage are history in the making.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They not only provide an emotional connection to our past, but also serve as inspiration and anchors for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, building owners also have a part to play in conservation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When we started out in the 1980s, many building owners did not see the value of conservation and, in fact, had to be persuaded quite hard at times to conserve their buildings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It was seen as a burden with additional cost, hurting their property rights, and many were reluctant to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But now we are seeing a change of mindset and, increasingly, more owners are becoming more receptive to the idea of conserving their buildings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our collective efforts at conserving and revitalising our built heritage have slowly gained recognition at the international level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These recognise and encourage public-private initiatives in restoring structures of heritage value in the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Page: 74 URA's conservation programme was also conferred the distinguished Urban Land Institute 2006 Global Award for Excellence in recognition of its works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And last year, Singapore's oldest Teochew temple, the Yueh Hai Ching temple at Phillip Street, which was established in 1826, also received the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Cultural Heritage Conservation Award (Merit).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And, of course, we witnessed the inscription of the Singapore Botanic Gardens as our first UNESCO World Heritage site.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There have been hits-and-misses and we need to do a lot more work on the road ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Going forward, we will continue to add to this list and expand our heritage spaces, even as we strive to transform our city to meet our future needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even for people who have not lived there before, they look at Dakota Crescent and either see a reflection of their early childhood, or, for younger people, they see it as an opportunity or a window into the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that is why the National Heritage Board (NHB) has worked on several initiatives to commemorate the heritage of Dakota Crescent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: NHB is also working on a video documentary of the estate, which will be uploaded on NHB's heritage portal, Roots.sg.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Community groups have also been active in their efforts to commemorate Dakota Crescent by collecting individual memories, conducting tours and documenting the history of the estate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Beyond these efforts, our planners are open to looking at the different ways in which the area can be redeveloped and rejuvenated, while retaining its distinctive identity and character.
